days.title: Prokaryotic vs Eukaryotic Cells
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish prokaryotic from eukaryotic cells.
  • Identify key structural differences.
  • Give examples of each cell type.
  • Explain evolutionary significance.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Prokaryote — a cell without a membrane-bound nucleus.
  • Eukaryote — a cell with a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
  • Nucleoid — the region in prokaryotes where DNA is concentrated.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Defining Features

FeatureProkaryoteEukaryote
NucleusAbsent (nucleoid)Present
Membrane-bound organellesAbsentPresent
Ribosomes70S80S
Cell size1–5 µm10–100 µm
DNACircular, nakedLinear, histone-bound
Cell wallPeptidoglycan (bacteria)Cellulose (plants), chitin (fungi)

B. Examples

  • Prokaryotes: Bacteria (E. coli), Archaea
  • Eukaryotes: Plants, animals, fungi, protists

C. Evolutionary Significance

Prokaryotes appeared ~3.5 billion years ago; eukaryotes ~1.5 billion years ago. The endosymbiotic theory explains how eukaryotes arose from prokaryotes engulfing smaller prokaryotes.

💬 Let's Discuss

All cells share four things: a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA. What separates the two great groups of life is where the DNA is kept and how the inside is organized.

Prokaryotes ("before nucleus") — bacteria and archaea — keep their single circular chromosome in an unwalled area called the nucleoid. They have no membrane-bound organelles, their ribosomes are small (70S), and they are tiny, usually 1–5 µm. Many also carry extra small DNA rings called plasmids, which can hold genes for antibiotic resistance. Their small size is an advantage: a high surface-area-to-volume ratio lets nutrients reach every part quickly, so some bacteria can divide every 20 minutes.

Eukaryotes ("true nucleus") — protists, fungi, plants and animals — enclose linear chromosomes wrapped around histone proteins inside a nucleus. They have membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, ER and Golgi, larger 80S ribosomes, and are usually 10–100 µm. The membranes divide the cell into compartments, so different chemical reactions can happen at the same time without interfering with each other — the way a house has a kitchen and a bedroom.

This difference has real medical uses. Antibiotics such as streptomycin attack 70S ribosomes, so they stop bacterial protein synthesis but leave our 80S ribosomes alone.

Common mistake: "Prokaryotes have no DNA" or "prokaryotes have no ribosomes." They have both — they just lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Another trap: yeast is a single-celled organism, but it is a eukaryote (a fungus).

pairs.why: A true, membrane-bound nucleus defines a eukaryote.
Prokaryotic DNA lies in the nucleoid, a region with no membrane.
Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are the larger 80S type.
Prokaryotes have smaller 70S ribosomes.
Most prokaryotes are only 1–5 micrometers long.
Eukaryotic cells are usually 10–100 micrometers.

scenarios.text: A cell has no membrane-bound nucleus.
scenarios.explanation: No membrane-bound nucleus is the defining feature of prokaryotes.

scenarios.text: A cell has mitochondria and ER.
scenarios.explanation: Mitochondria and ER are membrane-bound organelles found only in eukaryotes.

scenarios.text: A bacterium.
scenarios.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes.

scenarios.text: A cell with linear chromosomes bound to histones.
scenarios.explanation: Linear chromosomes with histones are found in eukaryotic nuclei.

scenarios.text: An organism with a nucleoid region.
scenarios.explanation: A nucleoid region instead of a nucleus means prokaryote.

scenarios.text: A plant leaf cell.
scenarios.explanation: Plant cells have a nucleus and organelles, so they are eukaryotic.

questions.text: Which structure is present in eukaryotic cells but absent in prokaryotic cells?
questions.explanation: Both cell types have ribosomes, membranes and DNA; only eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus.

questions.text: What type of ribosomes do prokaryotes have?
Which of the following is a prokaryote?
questions.explanation: E. coli is a bacterium; yeast, onion cells and neurons are eukaryotic.

takeaways: Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotes have one.
Prokaryotic DNA is circular and naked; eukaryotic DNA is linear and histone-bound.
Endosymbiotic theory explains the origin of eukaryotic organelles.

days.title: Plant vs Animal Cells
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Compare plant and animal cell structures.
  • Identify structures unique to each.
  • Relate structure to function.
  • Explain why certain organelles are more abundant in specific cells.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Cell wall — rigid outer layer in plant cells (cellulose).
  • Central vacuole — large water-storage organelle in plants.
  • Chloroplast — site of photosynthesis in plants.
  • Centriole — aids in cell division in animals.

📚 Lesson Content

Structures Unique to Plant Cells

  • Cell wall — cellulose; provides support and shape
  • Chloroplasts — photosynthesis
  • Central vacuole — stores water; maintains turgor pressure
  • Plasmodesmata — channels between plant cells

Structures Unique to Animal Cells

  • Centrioles — organize spindle fibers during cell division
  • Lysosomes — abundant in animal cells (plants have fewer)
  • Flagella/cilia — movement (some animal cells)

Structures in BOTH

  • Plasma membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, ER, Golgi, ribosomes, cytoskeleton

💬 Let's Discuss

Plant and animal cells are both eukaryotic, so they share the nucleus, mitochondria, ER, Golgi, ribosomes and plasma membrane. Their differences make sense once you remember how each organism lives.

A plant cannot walk to find food or run from danger, so it must make its own food and support its own weight. That explains its three special structures. The cell wall made of cellulose gives a rigid box shape and protects against bursting. Chloroplasts make sugar from sunlight. The large central vacuole stores water, ions and pigments; when it is full, it pushes against the wall and creates turgor pressure that keeps leaves and young stems firm. A wilted kangkong leaf is simply a plant whose vacuoles have lost water. Plant cells also connect to their neighbors through channels called plasmodesmata.

An animal cell has no wall, so it can change shape — think of a white blood cell squeezing out of a capillary or a muscle cell contracting. Animal cells usually have centrioles, which help organize spindle fibers during division, and many lysosomes that digest food particles and worn-out parts. Animals store energy as glycogen; plants store it as starch.

Common mistakes: (1) "Plant cells have no mitochondria." They do — chloroplasts make sugar, but mitochondria still convert it into ATP. (2) "Only plant cells have vacuoles." Animal cells have vacuoles too; they are just small and temporary. The difference is the single large central vacuole.

pairs.why: Only plants have a cellulose cell wall for rigid support.
Chloroplasts for photosynthesis are found in plant cells.
The single large central vacuole that maintains turgor is a plant feature.
Centrioles that organize spindle fibers are typical of animal cells.
Animal cells rely on many lysosomes for intracellular digestion.
Both plant and animal cells need mitochondria for ATP.
Both are eukaryotic, so both have a nucleus.
All cells, plant or animal, have ribosomes.

scenarios.text: A cell has a large central vacuole and chloroplasts.
scenarios.explanation: A large central vacuole together with chloroplasts identifies a plant cell.

scenarios.text: A cell has centrioles for spindle fiber formation.
scenarios.explanation: Centrioles are characteristic of animal cells.

scenarios.text: A cell has a plasma membrane and nucleus.
scenarios.explanation: Every eukaryotic cell has a plasma membrane and nucleus.

scenarios.text: A cell has a rigid cell wall.
scenarios.explanation: A rigid cellulose cell wall is found in plant cells.

scenarios.text: A cell has mitochondria.
scenarios.explanation: Both plant and animal cells need mitochondria to make ATP.

scenarios.text: A cell contains plasmodesmata.
scenarios.explanation: Plasmodesmata are channels through plant cell walls.

questions.text: Which of the following is found ONLY in plant cells?
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts are found only in plant cells; mitochondria, nucleus and ribosomes are in both.

questions.text: Which organelle helps organize spindle fibers during animal cell division?
questions.explanation: Centrioles help organize the spindle in animal cells.

questions.text: What is the main function of the central vacuole in plant cells?
questions.explanation: The central vacuole stores water and creates turgor pressure against the wall.

takeaways: Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a central vacuole.
Animal cells have centrioles and abundant lysosomes.
Both cell types share plasma membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, ER, Golgi, and ribosomes.

days.title: Plant & Animal Tissue Types
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Classify the four main animal tissue types.
  • Describe the three main plant tissue systems.
  • Relate tissue structure to function.
  • Locate tissues within the organism.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Tissue — a group of similar cells performing a specific function.
  • Epithelial tissue — covers body surfaces, lines cavities.
  • Connective tissue — binds, supports, protects.
  • Muscle tissue — contracts for movement.
  • Nervous tissue — transmits electrical signals.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Animal Tissues

TypeFunctionLocation
EpithelialCovering, lining, protection, absorptionSkin, intestine lining
ConnectiveBinding, support, transportBone, blood, cartilage, fat
MuscleMovementSkeletal, smooth, cardiac muscle
NervousSignalingBrain, spinal cord, nerves

B. Plant Tissues

SystemTissueFunction
DermalEpidermis, cuticleProtection
GroundParenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchymaPhotosynthesis, support
VascularXylem, phloemTransport

💬 Let's Discuss

A tissue is a group of similar cells working together for one function. Animals have only four basic tissue types, and you can sort almost any example by asking, "What is its main job?"

Epithelial tissue covers and lines — skin, the lining of your mouth and intestines, the walls of air sacs. Its cells are packed tightly with almost no space between them, forming a barrier. Connective tissue supports, binds and connects; its cells are scattered in a large amount of material called the matrix. That is why bone, cartilage, tendons, fat and even blood (with liquid plasma as its matrix) are all connective. Muscle tissue contracts: skeletal (voluntary), cardiac (heart) and smooth (walls of organs). Nervous tissue carries electrical signals through neurons, supported by glial cells.

Plants have three tissue systems. The dermal system (epidermis) is the protective outer layer, often coated with a waxy cuticle that reduces water loss. The vascular system transports: xylem carries water and minerals up from roots, while phloem carries sugars from leaves to where they are needed. The ground system fills the rest and does photosynthesis, storage and support. All of these come from meristems, regions of dividing cells at root and shoot tips.

Common mistake: calling blood a "liquid organ" or muscle tissue. Blood is connective tissue because its cells float in a matrix (plasma). Another trap is mixing up xylem and phloem: remember "xylem = water goes up; phloem = food."

pairs.why: Epithelium forms sheets that cover outer surfaces and line cavities.
Connective tissue has scattered cells in a matrix and binds and supports.
Muscle cells contain contractile proteins that shorten to move parts.
Neurons in nervous tissue conduct electrical impulses.
The epidermis is the dermal tissue covering the plant.
Vascular tissue is made of xylem (water) and phloem (sugar).
Ground tissue does photosynthesis, storage and support.

scenarios.text: Lines the inside of the small intestine.
scenarios.explanation: The intestinal lining is a sheet of epithelial cells.

scenarios.text: Transmits signals in the brain.
scenarios.explanation: Neurons in the brain belong to nervous tissue.

scenarios.text: Blood and bone.
scenarios.explanation: Blood and bone have cells in a matrix — connective tissue.

scenarios.text: Skeletal muscle fibers.
scenarios.explanation: Skeletal muscle fibers are muscle tissue.

scenarios.text: Transports water in plants.
scenarios.explanation: Xylem, part of vascular tissue, carries water.

scenarios.text: Outer protective layer of a leaf.
scenarios.explanation: The epidermis, a dermal tissue, protects the leaf surface.

questions.text: Which animal tissue covers and lines body surfaces?
questions.explanation: Epithelial tissue covers body surfaces and lines cavities.

questions.text: Which plant tissue transports water and minerals?
questions.explanation: Xylem moves water and minerals upward; phloem moves sugars.

questions.text: Blood is an example of which tissue type?
questions.explanation: Blood is connective tissue: its cells are suspended in plasma, a liquid matrix.

takeaways: Animals have four main tissue types: epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous.
Plants have three tissue systems: dermal, ground, vascular.
Structure of each tissue reflects its specific function.

days.title: Cell Modifications & Specialization
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe examples of cell modifications.
  • Explain how modifications enable specialized functions.
  • Relate structure to function at the cellular level.
  • Recognize cell modifications in real-world tissues.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Cell modification — a structural change that enables a specialized function.
  • Surface-area-to-volume ratio — the reason cells modify their surfaces.
  • Differentiation — process by which cells become specialized.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Examples of Cell Modifications

CellModificationFunction
Intestinal cellMicrovilliIncrease surface area for absorption
Root hair cellRoot hairs (elongations)Increase surface area for water/mineral absorption
Nerve cellLong axon, dendritesTransmit signals over long distances
Red blood cellBiconcave, no nucleusMaximize O₂ carrying capacity
Sperm cellFlagellumMotility
Guard cellBean-shaped, thick wallsOpen/close stomata

B. Why Modifications?

Cells modify their structure to maximize surface area, minimize diffusion distance, or perform specialized tasks. This is the cellular basis of differentiation.

💬 Let's Discuss

Every cell in your body has the same DNA, yet a neuron looks nothing like a red blood cell. During development, cells switch on different sets of genes, a process called differentiation, and their shape becomes fitted to their job. The key idea is simple: structure fits function.

Many modifications increase surface area. Cells lining the small intestine have microvilli, tiny finger-like folds of the membrane that multiply the absorbing surface many times — like how a crumpled towel holds more water than a flat sheet. In plants, root hairs are long, thin outgrowths of epidermal cells that reach into soil to absorb water and minerals.

Other modifications help with movement and communication. A sperm cell has a flagellum to swim and many mitochondria in its midpiece to power it. Cells lining the airways have cilia that sweep mucus and dust upward. A motor neuron can have an axon about a meter long so a signal travels from your spinal cord to your toes without passing through extra cells.

Some cells even give things up. Mature red blood cells lose their nucleus and most organelles, leaving room for more hemoglobin; their biconcave disc shape increases surface area and lets them bend through narrow capillaries. In leaves, pairs of bean-shaped guard cells swell or shrink to open and close stomata, balancing CO₂ intake against water loss.

Common mistake: confusing cilia and microvilli. Cilia move things; microvilli only absorb.

pairs.why: Microvilli fold the membrane outward, greatly increasing absorptive surface.
Root hairs extend into the soil to absorb water and minerals.
A long axon carries impulses over long distances in one cell.
The biconcave shape and missing nucleus allow more hemoglobin and better O₂ exchange.
The flagellum whips to propel the sperm cell.
Guard cells change shape to open or close the stoma.

scenarios.text: An intestinal cell has many tiny projections on its surface.
scenarios.explanation: Many tiny surface projections that absorb nutrients are microvilli.

scenarios.text: A root cell has a long, thin extension.
scenarios.explanation: The long extension of a root epidermal cell is a root hair.

scenarios.text: A red blood cell lacks a nucleus.
scenarios.explanation: Without a nucleus, a red blood cell has more room for hemoglobin to carry O₂.

scenarios.text: A nerve cell is very long.
scenarios.explanation: A long nerve cell carries signals over large distances.

scenarios.text: A sperm cell has a tail-like structure.
scenarios.explanation: The sperm's tail is a flagellum.

scenarios.text: A pair of bean-shaped cells controls gas exchange on a leaf.
scenarios.explanation: Guard cells regulate the opening of stomata for gas exchange.

questions.explanation: Microvilli increase the surface area available for absorption.

questions.text: Which modification allows sperm cells to swim?
questions.explanation: The flagellum lets sperm swim; cilia move fluid over a surface.

questions.text: Why do red blood cells lack a nucleus?
questions.explanation: Losing the nucleus makes room for more hemoglobin, so more oxygen can be carried.

takeaways: Cell modifications are structural changes enabling specialized functions.
Increasing surface area is a common modification (microvilli, root hairs).
Some modifications maximize function by losing structures (RBCs lose nuclei).
Differentiation produces specialized cells from unspecialized ones.
